question: Does gradient-mass coverage -- the metric this subfield selects masks by -- predict accuracy?
design: Three masks spanning 0.55 to 1.77 mass/token, trained identically (lr 1e-5 constant, 120 steps, 32 rollouts/step, 3 seeds each) and evaluated on MATH500. Statistics at the seed level.
finding: Gradient-mass coverage anti-predicts accuracy. Ranked by mass/token the order is v0c > vanilla > v0; ranked by accuracy it is exactly reversed. The arm that best satisfies the selection criterion (v0c, 1.77 mass/token) is statistically indistinguishable from not training at all (+0.008 over base, p=0.570), while the arm that fails it worst (v0, 0.55) learns most (+0.059). v0c vs v0 is -0.051, p=0.022.
mechanism: High divergence marks arbitrariness as readily as it marks information. Prose tokens diverge because phrasing is underdetermined -- many wordings are correct, so teacher and student disagree without either being wrong, and matching the teacher's word choice teaches no mathematics. Notation tokens agree because they are determined; training there reinforces correct computation without fighting over style.
consequence: DEAR-style gradient-mass coverage (entropy 39.1%, random 35.9% are the published targets) should not be used to select or justify a mask without an accuracy check. Here it would have picked the worst of three arms.
caveat: One learning rate, one benchmark, three seeds, one model pair. The ordering is clean but the mechanism is inferred, not demonstrated.
